habit_line: Focus habit: Try - Ask the child to test one example, or a smaller case, before deciding. Say: “Pick one example and test it. What happens?” Do not give the answer first: ask the prompt, wait, and give a hint only if the child is stuck.

say: How long is your pencil? “About this long” is not good enough. Today we measure carefully with equal units so everyone gets the same answer.
do: Focus habit: Try - Ask the child to test one example, or a smaller case, before deciding. Say: “Pick one example and test it. What happens?” Do not give the answer first: ask the prompt, wait, and give a hint only if the child is stuck.

say: I hold up two objects. Predict: which is longer? Now lay them side by side to check. Let me try three objects. Can you put them in order from shortest to longest?
Estimate: how many cubes long is your pencil? Write your guess before measuring.
stuck: Stuck: start at the zero end of the object, with no gaps.
Cubes overlap: “Are your cubes touching but not on top of each other?”
For pairs who want more: measure the same object with a different unit and compare the two numbers.

say: “A pencil is 6 cubes long and a book is 9 cubes long. How many cubes longer is the book? I draw two bars. The difference is 9 − 6 = 3.”

“1 clip is as long as 2 erasers. A pen is 4 clips long. How many erasers? 4 clips and each clip is 2 erasers: 4 + 4 = 8 erasers. A bigger unit gives a smaller number, so erasers (shorter) give a bigger number.”
“Rules for measuring: equal units, no gaps, no overlaps, start at zero.”

do: Ask: “Where does your object start? Is it at zero?”
Ask: “Why did you get a different number from your partner?”
Ask: “Is a bigger unit going to give a bigger number or a smaller number? Why?”
stuck: Hint 1: “Line the object up with zero.”
Hint 2: “Draw two bars and mark the difference.”
Hint 3: “Make the story with real cubes.”

say: “Why did you and your partner get different numbers of hand spans?”
“Why must the cubes have no gaps or overlaps?”
ask: “Why did you and your partner get different numbers of hand spans?”
Hands are different sizes, so hand spans are not equal units. Equal units laid end to end with no gaps or overlaps give a fair count.

say: “You measured fairly today and you can say why equal units matter.”

l9-title.note: Objective: Compare and order lengths, measure with equal units and with a centimetre ruler (also when the object does not start at 0), and change a length from one unit to another in both directions. Materials: Linking cubes or paper cube strips, paper clips, erasers, objects to measure, a cm ruler for each child, mini whiteboards. Online: Print the cube strip at the back of the workbook; measure household objects. Time plan: opening 0 to 2, warm-up 2 to 8 (game 2 to 6, quick questions 6 to 8; ask questions 1 to 3, and 4 and 5 only if you are on time), sneak-peek puzzles 8 to 12, explore 12 to 27, teaching 27 to 37 (click to reveal each step and answer), brain break 37 to 41, worksheet 41 to 72 with short teaching before each page and a check-together slide after it (a 30-second stand-and-stretch reset after the page-1 check, taken from that slot; the last 4 minutes check page 2, after a 1-minute stand-up stretch), talk time 72 to 79, exit ticket 79 to 85, look-back 85 to 88, then flex time and goodbye 88 to 90 (this is the buffer: if you are behind, use it; do not start anything new). Think harder, Go further and the Investigation are for every child to choose, any time or at home. Nobody is told which page they should be on. SPINE: Today's tool is Act it out. Use counters, paper or people to show it. Look for where you use it. Point at the card on page 1 of the workbook. HABIT: Focus habit: Try. Ask the child to test one example, or a smaller case, before deciding. Say: "Pick one example and test it. What happens?" Do not give the answer first: ask the prompt, wait, and give a hint only if the child is stuck.

l9-tool.note: SPINE: Show for about 20 seconds, inside the opening. Today's tool is Act it out. Use counters, paper or people to show it. Look for where you use it. Point at the card on page 1 of the workbook.

l9-warm1.note: Minutes 2 to 6. Longer or shorter? Hold up two objects. Predict, then check by laying them side by side. Order three objects.

l9-warm2.note: Minutes 6 to 8. Read each question aloud, give thinking time, take answers, then click to show the answer. Ask "How do you know?" each time. Answers: 1) The ribbon (7 cubes is more than 4 cubes). 2) 3 cubes (7 − 4 = 3; or count on from 4 to 7). 3) Crayon (5), pencil (7), pen (9). 4) Line up one end of each object at the same starting line, then look at the other end. Watch for children who say "the pen is longest because it has the biggest number" without saying the units are the same: praise it, then add "because they were all measured in the same cubes". Ask questions 1 to 3. Ask 4 and 5 only if the clock at minute 6 is on time. The 4-minute sneak-peek puzzles follow on the next slide.

l9-warmcheck.note: Minutes 8 to 12 (4 minutes). SAY (about 26 words, once): "Two sneak-peek puzzles: ideas we have not learnt yet. A guess is a great start, and I do not know is welcome. Nobody is marked." Question 1 is an access question: every child can try it with objects, a drawing or counting, so everyone starts with a win. Question 2 makes you think. Children try both on their own paper (about a minute each). Then everyone answers ONCE, after the second question: face to face, each child keeps the paper low so only the tutor sees it; online, children say the answers together on three (nothing is held up to the camera). There are no private chat messages. Never use boards or paper held up in front of the group or to the camera, and never read out or compare anyone's answer. Do not write scores down or announce them. Then click to show each answer to the whole group and say "Lots of us had a different idea, and that is fine." Look for good ideas to praise in a later lesson; do not keep a list of who found question 2 easy. When the worksheet starts (minute 41) invite the WHOLE group (“When you have finished Start here, you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation”), never one child by name. Everyone joins Explore and the Mini-lesson. Answers: 1) Ribbon A, by 2 squares (5 − 3). Draw or count the squares. 2) More. A shorter pencil covers less, so she needs more of them.

l9-explore1.note: Minutes 12 to 17. Pairs work with the materials: Linking cubes or paper cube strips, paper clips, erasers, objects to measure. Measure a pencil, a book and a shoe with cubes. Estimate first, then measure and compare with the guess. Then measure the same book with hand spans and compare with a partner. Online: Print the cube strip at the back of the workbook; measure household objects. Go further (what-if) is on this slide from the start: any pair may choose it at any time, so nobody waits. The tutor does not choose who and does not announce it. Answers: A bigger number (a shorter unit needs more of them). Open: accept any measured numbers if the shorter unit has the bigger count. The cube strip (Strip A) is cut out before the lesson (parents are asked in the materials message), so no cutting is needed in class. (parents are asked in the materials message), so no cutting is needed in class.

l9-explore2.note: Minutes 17 to 27. Let pairs keep working and move around the room (or breakout rooms). Gather them to answer these. Answers: 1) Open answers. 2) Equal units laid end to end give a fair count. 3) Hands are different sizes.

l9-teach1.note: Teach: the idea and why. Hold up a real pencil and some cubes. Click 1: six equal cubes from the very end of the pencil, touching. Click 2: the same pencil with gaps. Ask: "Is the pencil really 4 cubes long? Did it shrink?" (No: the gaps are length we did not count.) Click 3: big and small blocks. Ask: "If Ali says 4 blocks and Mei says 6 cubes, who has the longer pencil?" (We cannot tell: the units are not the same.) Click 4: read the rule together. Think-aloud: "Rules for measuring: equal units, no gaps, no overlaps, start at the end. If I break a rule, my number is not fair." Link back to the explore: "This is why you and your partner got different numbers of hand spans."

l9-we1.note: Worked example. Before each click ask the group to predict. Step 1 then the yellow highlight: "I line up the left ends, like a race start. Red goes further. The part that sticks out is the difference: 3 cubes. 8 take away 5 is 3." Step 2 then the long bar: "End to end means one after the other, so I add: 8 + 5 = 13." Step 3 then the cut bar: "If I cut 3 cubes off red, 8 − 3 = 5, the same as blue." Common mistake: answering "8" to "how much longer" (the length, not the difference). Point at the highlighted part.

l9-try1.note: Children write on their own paper and say the answer together on three (online: nothing is held up to the camera). Never ask for boards or paper held up in front of the group or to the camera. Then click. a) 9 − 6 = 3. b) 9 + 6 = 15. c) 10 − 4 = 6. Ask for a volunteer (never a named child) to show the part that sticks out on their bars for a, or show it yourself. A child who writes 9 for a has given the length, not the difference.

l9-teachcm.note: Teach. Give out rulers. "Cubes are our own unit. Everyone in the world uses the same unit: the centimetre. A ruler is a row of centimetres stuck together." Show that each space from one mark to the next is 1 cm (a fingertip wide). Click 1 and 2. Click 3 shows the jumps: "The number 7 tells us 7 spaces from 0." Click 4: "We count spaces, not marks. If I counted the marks from 0 to 7 I would get 8, which is wrong." Some rulers have a blank bit before 0: show where 0 is on yours.

l9-we2.note: Worked example (a ruler that does not start at 0, as if the end of the ruler were broken). Ask first: "How long is the key?" Many children say 9. Click 1: "9 is where the key ends, not how long it is. It started at 2, not 0." Click 2 and the jumps: count the spaces aloud together. Click 3: "Another way: from 0 to 9 is 9 spaces, but the first 2 spaces are not under the key. 9 − 2 = 7." Check by sliding a real key or pencil so it starts at 0. Think-aloud: "Where does it start? Where does it end? I count the spaces in between."

l9-try2.note: Own paper, ticked against the answer slide. a) The eraser goes from 2 to 6: 4 spaces, 4 cm (6 − 2 = 4). b) 11 − 6 = 5 cm. c) 4 − 1 = 3 cm. A child who writes 6, 11 or 4 is reading the end mark only: ask "Where does it start?" Let them check b and c on a real ruler.

l9-key.note: Say the key idea together. Common mistakes to watch for during the worksheet: (1) Counting a ribbon's squares carelessly or counting a square twice: touch each one. (2) Answering "how much longer" with the length instead of the difference. (3) "End to end" means add the two lengths. (4) Leaving gaps between cubes in Q2. (5) On a ruler, reading the end mark when the object does not start at 0.

l9-break.note: Four minutes. Online: children stay in view of the camera and move in place.

l9-ws1.note: Minutes 41 to 50. Walk around. Ask "How do you know?" before giving any help. Q1: check children count the squares (A 7, B 5, C 9) before answering. Q2: children copy the pencil, book and shoe numbers they found in Explore (no second measuring); only the "My choice" row is a new measure, so watch for gaps and for cubes not starting at the end of the object. The "How far off my guess was" column is the gap between guess and measure (for a guess of 8 and a measure of 6, it is 2). At minute 41 read questions 1 and 2 aloud, then pairs read the rest. The workbook says: "After question 3 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder." Never announce who is on which page and never name a child in front of the group; invite the WHOLE group at once, for example: "When you have finished Start here, you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation." Do not split a pair unless both children agree.

l9-ws1ans.note: Click each answer after a pair explains theirs. Q1: A has 7 squares, B has 5, C has 9. c) 7 − 5 = 2. d) 7 + 5 = 12. e) C cut 2 shorter: 9 − 2 = 7, the same as A. Q2a: "If the cubes were different sizes, the numbers would not mean the same thing, so we could not compare." Reset (about 30 seconds, taken from this slot): when the answers are checked, everyone stands, reaches up high, shakes out their hands, takes one slow breath and sits down again, then page 2. Skip it if you are more than a minute behind.

l9-teachunit.note: Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q3 and Q4). 1 clip = 2 erasers here and on the worksheet. Use real clips and erasers if you have them (or draw). Click 1: the clips. Click 2: the erasers. Ask: "Is the stick longer when we use erasers?" (No, it is the same stick.) Click 3. Think-aloud: "A bigger unit covers more of the stick each time, so I need fewer of them. A smaller unit gives a bigger number." Your turn: write it on your own paper, then click. "Tom needs fewer steps for the same path, so each of his steps is bigger." Do not tell them the Q3 answer: it is the same idea with hand spans.

l9-teachconv.note: Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q4 goes both ways). Left side, click 1: draw 2 erasers under each clip. Click 2: count in 2s along the erasers: 2, 4, 6, 8. Think-aloud: "4 clips, and every clip is 2 erasers, so 2 and 2 and 2 and 2: 8 erasers." Right side, click 3: ring the erasers in 2s. Click 4: "6 erasers make 3 groups of 2, so 3 clips. I check: 2 + 2 + 2 = 6." Click 5: the summary. Ask: "Changing to erasers, did the number get bigger or smaller? Why?" The teaching slides and the worksheet both use 1 clip = 2 erasers, so the worksheet Q4 is the same method (5 clips; 12 erasers).

l9-teachmore.note: Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q5). Click to build each bar; before each click ask "Longer or shorter than red? By how much?" Think-aloud: "Blue is 2 longer than red, so I draw red's 7 and 2 more: 9. Green is 3 shorter than red, so I draw red's 7 and cross off 3: 4. End to end: 7 + 9 = 16, and 4 more is 20." Common mistake: adding 7 + 2 + 3 for the total, using the differences instead of the lengths.

l9-ws2.note: Children work alone. Note who may need a short catch-up next lesson (never in front of the group). Q4: the worksheet says 1 clip = 2 erasers (not 3 as in our teaching), so check children use groups of 2.

l9-ws2ans.note: Click each answer after a child explains. Q3: 6 spans and 8 spans for the same desk; fewer spans means each one covers more, so Ali's hand span is longer. Q4a: 5 clips, each 2 erasers: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. Q4b: 12 erasers in groups of 2: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12 is 6 groups, so 6 clips. Q5: Ali 8 + 3 = 11, Ben 8 − 2 = 6, together 8 + 11 + 6 = 25. Q6: b) count the spaces from 3 to 8, or 8 − 3 = 5; a child who writes 8 has read the end mark only. Each child needs a cm ruler. First, everyone stands up and stretches for about a minute (reach up high, touch your toes, shake out your hands) so there is some movement before talk time.

l9-stretch.note: For any pair that chooses to try more (these are on the slide only; Think harder T1 to T4 are in the workbook). Answers: 1) 5 cubes each (5 + 5 + 5 = 15) and 2 cuts: 3 pieces need only 2 cuts. 2) Ben. Six clips of 2 cubes each: 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 12 cubes. 3) The 11 cm mark (3 + 8 = 11).

l9-challenge.note: For any pair that chooses Go further. Use it as a pair choice, or with volunteers in talk time (never call a child by name). Ask for the reason every time. Q3 is open: there is no single right answer, so ask children to check each other's work. Answers: 1) 20 cubes (18 + 2 gaps). With 5 carriages: 30 + 4 gaps = 34 cubes. There is always 1 gap fewer than carriages. 2) 14, 10 and 6 cubes. 3) Open. Check that the link between the units is stated and the answer works. Example: 1 clip is as long as 4 cubes. A snake is 5 clips long. How many cubes long is it? Answer: 20 cubes.

l9-chdiag.note: Show this picture slide only if a pair asks for it, or is stuck on Go further. The pictures show each problem, not its answer. Ask: What do you notice? What do we know? What do we not know yet? Can you draw or build it? Do not point out the answer; wait for a child to find a pattern.

l9-chwalk.note: Use after pairs have tried. Reveal one answer at a time and ask a child to explain before you click. Many children stop at one answer: ask "Is there another way?" and "How do you know you found them all?" For Q3, ask two pairs to swap puzzles and solve each other's.

l9-skill1.note: Optional slide for pairs who finish early or ask for more. Show it only on request and never announce who is working on it. Children write the answer on their own paper and say it together on three; nothing is held up to the camera. Answers and tutor lines are for you only. Item 1 (Time: o'clock, half past and minutes in fives; tool of the day idea: Act it out). SAY: "Use a paper clock. Move the minute hand and count in fives." ASK: "Where is the minute hand at half past? How many minutes from the 12 to the 6?" LISTEN FOR: Each number on the clock is 5 minutes. ANSWER: a) 7:30 (half past 7). b) 8:30. c) 20 minutes (5, 10, 15, 20).

l9-talk.note: Minutes 72 to 79. Pairs talk for 2 minutes. Then ask for volunteers first ("Who would like to share?"), never call a child by name to answer, and say that passing is always fine. No tallies and no rankings. Praise the reasons, not only the answers.

l9-exit.note: Minutes 79 to 85. Answer: 6 cm (count the spaces from 3 to 9, or 9 − 3 = 6). A child who writes 9 has read the end mark only. Extension: Measure the same object with two different units and find the rule linking the two counts.

l9-reflect.note: SPINE: Minutes 85 to 88. Start the timer (120 seconds). Say: "Pick one problem from today. Question 1: did I answer the question? Question 2: does my answer make sense? Question 3: can I check it another way? Tick, write one line, or pass. If you are still stuck, tick the box and I will come." Children tick the Look back box on the Choose and look-back page of their workbook, or just tick on paper. A pass is always allowed. It is never marked, never collected in front of the group and never read out; the tutor may look at it afterwards. If a child ticks "I am still stuck", check in during the open session next lesson (a quick visit to the shared breakout room or a hand signal, with a parent nearby; never a direct message). Do not ask children to share. Praise a check you saw, not speed. Then stamp the journals. After the look-back, minutes 88 to 90 are flex time (the buffer): finish stamps, then goodbye. Do not start anything new. HABIT: Focus habit: Try. Ask the child to test one example, or a smaller case, before deciding. Say: "Pick one example and test it. What happens?" Do not give the answer first: ask the prompt, wait, and give a hint only if the child is stuck.
